Validation studies live in validation.json table plants_validation, never here.

A lower bound, not a typical life span. Francis: 'this long-lived species' and 'a planted tree more than 200 years old in St. Croix ... has reached 2 m d.b.h. and 25 m in height'. No upper age or mortality curve found. PROTA gives a rotation of 40 to 60 years, which is a harvest age, not a life span.
plantation trees (Francis, citing Lamb 1966) against usual seed age in the Agroforestree Database

Age at first flowering and fruiting. Francis: 'Flowering and fruiting of plantation trees starts at 12 to 13 years of age'. The Agroforestree Database: fertile seed 'sometimes as early as at 20 years of age, although usually it does not seed until it is 30-40 years old'. The Tropical Tree Seed Manual (genus) gives 10 to 25 years for open-grown dominant and codominant trees. The sources disagree by a factor of three; only dominant and codominant trees flower.

A Florida study (Howard, Nakahara and Williams 1995, Annales des Sciences Forestieres 52:283-286) is reported in search results to name thrips as the only insects seen on the flowers, but the paper was not opened (the publisher returned 403), so thrips are not entered here as a finding. seasonal; shortly before the rainy season, spring and early summer (a timing report, no cue tested)
Caribbean and Puerto Rico, as reported

Agroforestree Database: 'Flowering and fruiting are regular and annual, varying according to climate but taking place shortly before the rainy season'. Francis: flowering 'in spring and early summer'. No source tests day length, temperature or water as the trigger, so this is a timing correlation, not a cue a mechanism can read.
winged seed (samara) in a woody 5-valved capsule; about 8 to 10 months from flower to ripe fruit

Agroforestree Database: capsule 6 to 10 cm by 4 to 5 cm, each valve releases about 20 flat winged seeds 4 to 6 cm long. Francis: capsule may hold up to 60 seeds; 50 capsules in Puerto Rico averaged 39 +/- 1.3 seeds (19 to 56); usually one fruit per inflorescence. PROTA: about 10 times as many male as female flowers.
winged seeds, field observation as reported

PROTA: the seed wing makes it rotate when it falls and seeds are 'dispersed by wind as far as 500 m from the mother tree'. The Tropical Tree Seed Manual (genus Swietenia) says the seeds spiral downward and outward and 'usually land within 1 or 2 tree lengths of the mother tree'. The two disagree on distance by an order of magnitude; the 500 m is a maximum, the other a usual distance.
air-dried seeds, Puerto Rico; converted from seeds per kg

Converted from seeds per kg: Value from Francis's 'about 7,000 per kg' (Marrero 1949), 1000 g / 7000. Low and High from the Tropical Tree Seed Manual table for S. mahagoni, 5,400 to 7,800 seeds per kg (https://www.fs.usda.gov/nsl/Wpsm/Swietenia.pdf). The Agroforestree Database gives 3,350 to 3,500 seeds per kg (0.29 to 0.30 g), twice as heavy; whether wings are included is not stated by any of them.
no pretreatment; any moist medium; hypogeal; about 70 % germination, first seeds after about 18 days
tests in Puerto Rico (Marrero 1949, as reported by Francis); seed viability about 2 months at room temperature

Francis: 'No pregermination treatments are necessary ... The seeds will germinate in almost any moist media. An average of 70-percent germination was noted ... an average of 18 days passed before the first seeds germinated'. Seeds may be stored at room temperature for about 2 months. PROTA: germination 60 to 95 %, starting about 15 days after sowing. The Agroforestree Database: seeds lose much viability in 3 months, nearly all in 6. Seedlings need light and fail under dense shade (Agroforestree). No temperature or moisture thresholds for germination found.

saccharum_officinarum.title: Sugarcane
saccharum_officinarum.source: Filled by research unit 2810 from opened pages; every Value is researched or estimate with a URL or stated basis; rows without a source stay null with a searched: line in flags/plants.md.
rows: domesticated sugar crop; native range New Guinea and nearby islands; grown worldwide in the tropics

Wikipedia (Saccharum officinarum): stems 'can reach 5 metres', domesticated in New Guinea from S. robustum 'around 6,000 BP'; sugarcane is grown for cane stalk (Wikipedia, Sugarcane: 'average production of cane stalk stands at 60-70 tonnes per hectare'). A tall perennial grass, listed here as crop because the schema's tags are tree, crop, seagrass, mangrove.
sugarcane in general; the page is not specific to S. officinarum
Wikipedia (Sugarcane): 'It is a C4 plant, able to convert up to 1% of incident solar energy into biomass.' A reference page, so Evidence 3; no plant-physiology paper was opened for the pathway.
plantations worldwide (stem cuttings, ratoons); wild-type rhizome behaviour from the species description

Wikipedia (Sugarcane): 'modern stem cutting has become the most common reproduction method'; 'after each harvest, the cane sends up new stalks, called ratoons'. Wikipedia (S. officinarum): 'A network of rhizomes forms under the soil which sends up secondary shoots near the parent plant.' The plantation crop is therefore clonal both by planting and by ratooning.
g dry mass per MJ PAR

Rio Largo, Alagoas, NE Brazil (9.5 S, 127 m), irrigated, humid megathermal climate; cultivar RB98710 (a modern hybrid, not a noble cane); plant crop sampled 169 to 439 days after planting; two row spacings

The text also gives 1.96 and 1.86 g MJ-1 on an intercepted global-radiation basis (first two samplings, dry leaves included). Basis is shoot dry mass per MJ intercepted PAR. Creole cane (a Java-ribbon-type hybrid) to c. 1790; Otaheite (Tahitian) cane from c. 1790 to 1792 in the West Indies; Bourbon cane (Bougainville collection, confused with Otaheite); ribbon canes from 1790 to 1810
historical and genetic reports on Caribbean and Louisiana cane before about 1830; none gives a measured field comparison, and the agronomy rows above describe modern hybrids

Canes of the Caribbean before about 1800: (1) Creole cane, the sole type for about 1,100 years in the Americas (introduced to Europe 711 CE, planted in the Americas 1506), ousted by Tahitian (Otaheite) cane c. 1790 (bioRxiv 2020, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.07.29.226852v1); (2) Otaheite cane, from Bougainville's Pacific voyages, first planted on Martinique and by 1792 spread to other West Indian islands 'supplanting the old Creole Cane' (Shields 2021 citing Caines 1801, https://davidsanfordshields.substack.com/p/issue-21-sugar-and-sorghum-part-4); (3) Bourbon cane, another Bougainville collection, 'sometimes confused' with Otaheite (same Shields page); no opened source gives a date or trait for Bourbon cane in the Caribbean; (4) a ribbon cane, Guinguam, appeared in the Caribbean between 1790 and 1810 and is described as a Sinense type from Java (bioRxiv). Identity: the bioRxiv authors report 'evidence for only a single type of Creole in the new world', conclude 'Java ribbon cane is the historical New World sugarcane known as Creole' and that 'Creole cane is an hybrid and not a single species'; the Creole cane of the plantations was therefore not a pure S. officinarum. Trait differences each source states: Otaheite versus Creole, juice yield about one third more, stems higher, thicker and more succulent, 'more luxuriant vegetation', lighter green, thicker stalks better as boiling fuel (Caines 1801 via Shields); Otaheite was vulnerable to cold, and Purple Ribbon (introduced to Georgia in 1814) 'substantially more cold tolerant than Otaheiti' (Shields); Creole 'is said to produce the most sugar, when perfectly ripened, but it requires a longer season' than the other kinds (Williams 1837 in Thornton's Glossary, https://wehd.com/thornton/Creole_cane.html); Creole 'not well suited to the Louisiana terrain' and ribbon cane introduced 1817 made cane an important crop there (Harris 2021, https://64parishes.org/cane-contemplations). No opened source states a ratooning difference between Creole and Otaheite; Shields says nothing on ratooning. Dates conflict among sources (c. 1790 bioRxiv, 1792 Shields).

forms.title: General plant growth forms (equations and their constants)
forms.source: 2808 research: each row from a page opened 2026-10-31; equation rows hold the equation in Note with Value null; constant rows hold Value, Low, High. Evidence 2 is the level the life DESIGN.md gives these forms; PLATFORM.md section 4 was outside this task's read list.
rows: Source: attenuation of PPFD in a canopy is approximated by Beer's law, with I the PPFD on a horizontal plane under cumulative leaf area index F from the canopy top, I0 the PPFD above the canopy, K the extinction coefficient (Monsi and Saeki 1953 as reviewed by Hirose 2005). The equation is an image on the page, so the exponential form I = I0 exp(-K F) is Beer's law written from those definitions, not transcribed. Monsi and Saeki 1953 itself was not opened.
full-sunlight canopies, LAI about 5; horizontal leaves 0.7 to 1.0, vertical leaves 0.3 to 0.5
Value is the K the review calls common for canopies in full sunlight; Low and High are the range across all cases it reports. Small randomly distributed horizontal leaves give K = 1 by theory.

Kd(z) = -d ln Ed(z)/dz; if Kd does not vary with depth, Ed(z) = Ed(0) exp(-Kd z), z positive downward from the surface. The page states the constant-Kd form is always an approximation. It is written for wavelength-resolved plane irradiance; applying it to PAR (PAR_z = PAR_0 exp(-Kd z)) is the design's use, and no seagrass-specific source was opened.
Norunda, Sweden, 1 Jan to 31 Oct 2004; daily ratio of PAR to shortwave

Value is the mean, Low and High the daily extremes at that site. A second measured site (Huaihe Valley, China) gave monthly means 0.37 to 0.43 and an annual mean 0.40, so the ratio is site and sky dependent.

RUE is defined as the biomass produced per unit of solar radiation intercepted or absorbed by the canopy (Caram et al. 2025, citing Monteith 1972 and 1977). The page writes it in words, not as an equation; the design's G = e I_abs is that definition applied.
g per MJ total solar energy
barley, potatoes, sugar beet, apples; Britain
Monteith 1977 abstract: these four crops form carbohydrate at about 1.4 g per MJ of solar energy (2.4% efficiency). This is per total solar energy, not per PAR, so it is not the design's e.
g DM per MJ intercepted PAR
C3 grass monocultures, aboveground; citing Monteith 1977 and Stockle and Kemanian 2009
Average RUE of C3 grass monocultures as reported by Caram et al. 2025; a secondary statement of a value from the cited works.
g DM per MJ intercepted PAR
C4 species under field conditions; values above 2.0 reported under abundant nitrogen and light

Range as stated by Caram et al. 2025, citing Sinclair and Muchow 1999, Kiniry et al. 2007 and Stockle and Kemanian 2009. No single value is given, so Value is null. Sugarcane has no row of its own in this page.
T in degrees C measured from 0; abstract form without Tmin

Abstract of Yan and Hunt 1999: r = Rmax ((Tmax - T)/(Tmax - Topt)) (T/Topt)^(Topt/(Tmax - Topt)), r the daily rate at temperature T, Rmax the rate at Topt. The page's markup lost the exponent layout; the structure is read from the order of the garbled terms and checks (r = Rmax at T = Topt, 0 at Tmax). The Tmin-shifted form that uses all three cardinal temperatures was not seen. The devRate manual lists beta forms with a base temperature (Yin et al. 1995; Shi et al. 2016) but none named for Yan and Hunt.
applies when Dr > RAW; Dr root zone depletion, mm

Ks = (TAW - Dr)/(TAW - RAW) for Dr > RAW, Ks = 1 for Dr <= RAW, with TAW = AWC x zr and RAW = p TAW (written MAD x TAW in the code documentation). FAO-56 Chapter 8 defines Ks as a dimensionless transpiration reduction factor in [0, 1], RAW = p TAW, and Ks = 1 when Dr is below RAW; its Eq 84 is an image, so the algebraic form is taken from the SWIM-RS documentation, which names FAO-56 as its source. p per crop is in FAO-56 Table 22, not opened.
ETc adj = Ks Kc ETo (Eq 81). FAO-56 says the dual form ETc adj = (Ks Kcb + Ke) ETo (Eq 80) is generally more valid because Ks affects only transpiration, not soil evaporation.

ETc = Kc ETo (Eq 58). Only three values describe the Kc curve: Kc ini and Kc mid, each constant over its stage, and Kc end at the end of the late season; Kc changes linearly between them over crop development and the late season. Kc values per crop are not in this row.
ECe of saturated-paste extract, mean root zone; two-segment line

Yr = 100 - b (ECe - a) for ECe above the threshold, 100 below it; Yr relative yield in percent, a salinity threshold in dS/m, b slope in percent per dS/m. The page attributes the two-line-segment response to Maas and Hoffman 1977 (Crop salt tolerance, current assessment). Source is the 1985 FAO revision, which may carry updated a and b; the 1977 paper was not opened.

'LLM states that the growth of an organism is constrained by the most limiting nutrient at that moment' (Tang and Riley 2021). The same paper credits Sprengel with proposing the law as early as 1826 and Liebig's 1840 book with making it popular, and notes Gorban et al. 2011 argue adaptive organisms are not limited by one substrate for long. Supports Rex's rule that among nutrients only the scarcest counts.
plant tissue analysis; critical level as usually defined

Critical concentration is usually defined as the tissue level that gives 90% of maximum yield or growth (Mosaic), and the UGA handbook calls a critical value the concentration below which deficiency occurs and the lower end of the sufficiency range. Neither page names Ulrich 1952 for the definition; the UGA page cites Ulrich 1961 for response curves. Other definitions exist (5 to 10% reduction), so the 90% is a convention.

R = RG + RM = gR G + mR W = gR dW/dt + mR W, with G the growth rate, W biomass, gR the growth respiration coefficient (mol CO2 per mol C) and mR the maintenance coefficient (mol CO2 per mol C per time); with photosynthesis P, dW/dt = (P - mR W)/(1 + gR) (Wendering and Nikoloski 2023; the page's markup is garbled so the algebra is the reconstruction in their text, not verbatim). Amthor 2000 calls the growth plus maintenance split the simplest form of the paradigm. McCree 1970 and Thornley 1970 were not opened (the Nature page refused); no coefficient values were found.
short-term response; often-assumed value, not a measured mean

Atkin and Tjoelker 2003: Q10 is often assumed to be 2.0 (respiration doubles per 10 C) but is not constant, declining near-linearly with rising temperature, and long-term acclimation is common. The abstract gives no range, so Low and High are null.
pantropical; trees with D at least 5 cm; height known

AGB = 0.0673 x (WD x H x D^2)^0.976 with D in cm, H in m, WD in g/cm3 (Chave et al. 2014, Eq 4 as implemented in the BIOMASS package, whose page gives the output in Mg). The paper was not opened (every full-text page refused), so the coefficients come from the package's page and the paper's own output unit is unconfirmed.
Coefficient of AGB = a (WD H D^2)^b; see allometry_agb_eq4.
Exponent b of AGB = a (WD H D^2)^b; see allometry_agb_eq4.
no height measured; E an environmental stress index from site coordinates

AGB = exp(-2.024 - 0.896 E + 0.920 ln(WD) + 2.795 ln(D) - 0.0461 (ln D)^2) per the BIOMASS page, which calls this a slight modification of Chave et al. 2014 Eq 7 (citing Rejou-Mechain et al. 2017). The page does not state the log base (natural log assumed here only for the written form). Not needed unless height is absent.

ETo = [0.408 Delta (Rn - G) + gamma (900/(T + 273)) u2 (es - ea)] / [Delta + gamma (1 + 0.34 u2)] (FAO-56 Eq 6). Rn net radiation and G soil heat flux in MJ m-2 d-1, T mean daily air temperature at 2 m in C, u2 wind speed at 2 m in m s-1, es - ea vapour pressure deficit in kPa, Delta slope of the vapour pressure curve and gamma the psychrometric constant in kPa per C. FAO-56 prints Eq 6 as an image; the form is read from the NCL code (labelled FAO 56 Eq 6) and Wikipedia for the constants 900 and 0.34, units from FAO-56 Ch 3. For daily steps G = 0 (Eq 42, per NCL).

light-use-efficiency crop model (CASA) applied to grassland NPP

e(x,t) = Te1(x,t) x Te2(x,t) x We(x,t) x emax: two temperature scalars and one moisture scalar multiply the maximum light-use efficiency (Zhang et al. 2017, applying CASA, Eq 7). Shows the multiplicative half of Rex's rule is a published practice; Potter et al. 1993 was not opened.
APSIM canola; radiation-based rate against water-supply rate

Daily biomass increase is the minimum of two potential rates: one set by intercepted radiation limited by temperature and nitrogen stresses, the other by soil water supply (Robertson et al., APSIM canola). A published crop model that uses a minimum, not a product, across the water pathway; the page gives no equations.
